questions.title: Bacterial spores: the one accurate statement
questions.question: Several bacteria that form spores are important human pathogens. Which one of the following is the most accurate statement about bacterial spores?

options.A: They are killed by boiling for 15 minutes
options.B: They are produced primarily by gram-negative cocci
options.C: They are formed primarily when the bacterium is exposed to antibiotics
options.D: They are produced by anaerobes only in the presence of oxygen
options.E: They are metabolically inactive yet can survive for years in that inactive state

explanations.A: Incorrect. Boiling for 15 minutes does not reliably kill bacterial endospores -- their heat resistance is exactly what makes them a sterilisation challenge; reliable destruction needs autoclaving (moist heat under pressure, roughly 121C) for an adequate hold time, not simple boiling.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Endospores are formed by certain Gram-positive rods (classically Bacillus and Clostridium species), not by Gram-negative cocci.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sporulation is triggered by nutrient limitation and other unfavourable environmental conditions, not by exposure to antibiotics.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sporulation is not restricted to anaerobes, nor is it specifically dependent on the presence of oxygen -- both aerobic (Bacillus) and anaerobic (Clostridium) spore-formers exist, and sporulation is driven by nutrient depletion, not an oxygen requirement.
explanations.E: Correct. The single most accurate statement here is that bacterial endospores are metabolically inactive (dormant) yet can survive for years in that inactive state -- this dormancy is exactly what gives spores their extraordinary resistance to heat, desiccation, radiation and chemicals, and it is the biological purpose of sporulation: to let the organism outlast harsh conditions until the environment improves and the spore can germinate back into an active vegetative cell. None of the other listed claims (boiling sensitivity, gram-negative-cocci origin, antibiotic trigger, obligatory aerobic formation) is correct.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that bacterial endospores are metabolically inactive yet can survive for years, rejecting false claims about boiling sensitivity, gram-negative-cocci origin, antibiotic-triggered formation, and an obligatory aerobic requirement.

questions.title: Plasmids play no direct role in bacterial cell division
questions.question: The following bacterial structures play a role in cell division EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this structure IS involved in cell division). The cell wall, via septum formation (new wall material laid down at the division site), is directly involved in splitting one bacterial cell into two.
explanations.B: Incorrect (involved in division). Mesosomes have classically been described as anchoring the bacterial chromosome and coordinating its segregation during cell division.
explanations.C: Incorrect (involved in division). The chromosome must replicate and segregate for cell division to succeed; it is central to the process, not peripheral to it.
explanations.D: Correct. Plasmids are accessory extrachromosomal DNA elements -- while they do get replicated and partitioned into daughter cells alongside the chromosome, they are not themselves structures that carry out or organise the mechanical process of cell division, unlike the cell wall's septum formation, the mesosome's classical chromosome-anchoring role, the chromosome's own segregation, or the cytoplasmic membrane's role in septum ingrowth. A plasmid's role is to carry accessory genes (e.g. antibiotic resistance), not to drive division itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect (involved in division). The cytoplasmic membrane grows inward at the division site (septum ingrowth) as part of splitting the cell in two.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that plasmids, unlike the cell wall, mesosomes, chromosome and cytoplasmic membrane, play no direct mechanical role in bacterial cell division.

questions.title: Protoplasts come from Gram-positive, not Gram-negative, bacteria
questions.question: Protoplasts have the following characters EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement). Protoplasts are indeed derived from Gram-positive bacteria -- since a Gram-positive cell has only peptidoglycan external to its membrane, removing that wall leaves a fully wall-less protoplast.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). A protoplast cannot replicate in its wall-less state; it depends on an osmotically protective medium just to survive.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement). Protoplasts must be maintained in an osmotically protective medium, or they lyse from unopposed osmotic pressure with no wall to resist it.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Protoplasts are NOT formed from Gram-negative bacteria -- treating a Gram-negative cell with lysozyme instead yields a spheroplast, since the outer membrane survives the treatment and leaves a residual outer layer. "Protoplast" specifically names the Gram-positive result, where nothing at all is left outside the membrane.
explanations.E: Incorrect (true statement). Protoplasts are indeed produced after treating a bacterium with lysozyme, which digests the peptidoglycan wall.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that protoplasts are formed from Gram-positive (not Gram-negative) bacteria after lysozyme treatment, cannot replicate, and require an osmotically protective medium.

questions.title: Corynebacterium diphtheriae stores metachromatic granules
questions.question: Storage granules are present in the cytoplasm of?

explanations.A: Incorrect. E. coli is not classically associated with prominent cytoplasmic storage granules on routine staining.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bacillus anthracis is notable for its antiphagocytic polypeptide capsule and its endospores, not for cytoplasmic storage granules.
explanations.C: Correct. Corynebacterium diphtheriae is the classic organism whose cytoplasm contains prominent storage (inclusion) granules -- metachromatic, or Babes-Ernst, granules composed largely of stored polyphosphate. These granules stain a different colour from the surrounding cytoplasm with certain dyes (e.g. methylene blue), which is a long-standing microscopic aid to identifying the organism, particularly in diphtheria diagnosis. Like other bacterial inclusion/storage granules, they serve as a nutrient reserve for the organism's own metabolism rather than any direct role in pathogenesis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Klebsiella is notable for its prominent polysaccharide capsule, not for cytoplasmic storage granules.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Corynebacterium diphtheriae as the classic organism whose cytoplasmic storage (metachromatic/Babes-Ernst) granules aid its microscopic identification.

questions.title: Spore formation: adverse conditions and nucleoprotein concentration
questions.question: Spore formation?

options.A: Occurs only in response to adverse environmental conditions
options.B: Initially starts with the assembling or local concentration of material. Presumably nucleoprotein

explanations.A: Incorrect alone (true but partial). Sporulation is indeed triggered by adverse/nutrient-limited conditions, but this is only one of the two correct statements combined in option D, not the complete answer by itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone (true but partial). Sporulation does begin with the assembly or local concentration of material, presumed to be nucleoprotein, at the future spore site -- but again, this alone is not the complete answer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sporulation is a survival mechanism, not a method of reproduction -- one vegetative cell forms one spore, which later germinates back into one vegetative cell; the spore count does not increase relative to the parent cells.
explanations.D: Correct. Both preceding statements are individually true: sporulation occurs specifically in response to adverse environmental conditions (most classically nutrient limitation), and it initially begins with the assembly or local concentration of material, presumed to be nucleoprotein, at the site where the spore will form. Since both A and B are accurate and the question asks which statements are correct, "A & B are correct" is the right combined answer, rather than either alone or the overreaching "all of these," since sporulation is specifically not a method of reproduction (option C).
explanations.E: Incorrect. This would require option C (reproduction) to also be true, but sporulation is not a reproductive mechanism, so "all of these" overreaches beyond the two genuinely correct statements (A and B).

questions.learning_objective: State that sporulation is triggered by adverse conditions and begins with nucleoprotein concentration at the spore site, while rejecting the claim that it is a method of reproduction.

questions.title: The nuclear membrane is absent from a prokaryotic cell
questions.question: Which of the following cellular structure is NOT found in prokaryotic cell?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A prokaryotic cell does have a "primitive nucleus" in the loose sense of an unbound nucleoid region holding its DNA -- this is present, just not membrane-bound.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Prokaryotic cells do have a comparatively simple enzyme system relative to eukaryotic cells; this is a genuine, if imprecise, feature that is present.
explanations.C: Correct. A prokaryotic cell has no nuclear membrane at all -- its DNA sits free in the cytoplasm within the unbound nucleoid region, unlike a eukaryotic cell, whose DNA is enclosed by a true nuclear envelope. This absence of a nuclear membrane is one of the single most defining features separating a prokaryotic cell from a eukaryotic one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Absence of mitochondria" is phrased here as a feature that IS found (i.e. a prokaryotic cell genuinely lacks mitochondria), so it does not answer the question of what structure is NOT found -- the absence of mitochondria is itself an accurate prokaryotic characteristic.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A definite answer (nuclear membrane) does exist among the options, so "none of these" is not applicable.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the nuclear membrane as the structure absent from a prokaryotic cell, distinguishing it from the nucleoid ("primitive nucleus"), the simple enzyme system, and the (true) absence of mitochondria.

questions.title: The bacterial chromosome is double-stranded and circular
questions.question: Bacterial chromosome is?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The bacterial chromosome is circular, but it is double-stranded DNA, not single-stranded.
explanations.B: Correct. The bacterial chromosome is a double-stranded, circular DNA molecule -- double-stranded like essentially all cellular genomic DNA, and circular (rather than the linear chromosomes of a eukaryotic nucleus), typically held free in the cytoplasm's nucleoid region rather than enclosed by a nuclear membrane. This double-stranded-and-circular combination is a standard, testable feature distinguishing bacterial genome organisation from the eukaryotic pattern.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The bacterial chromosome is circular, which this option gets right by elimination, but it wrongly describes it as single-stranded rather than double-stranded.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The bacterial chromosome is double-stranded, which this option gets right, but it wrongly describes it as linear -- it is circular.

questions.learning_objective: State that the bacterial chromosome is double-stranded and circular DNA.

questions.title: Vibrio cholerae is monotrichous
questions.question: Vibrio cholerae has a single polar flagellum. It is classified as being?

explanations.A: Correct. A single flagellum located at one pole of the cell is, by definition, the monotrichous arrangement. Vibrio cholerae, the cause of cholera, is a classic clinically relevant example of a monotrichous organism, and its single polar flagellum is what drives its characteristic rapid, darting motility. This links the abstract arrangement term back to a real pathogen, unlike the purely definitional flagellar-arrangement questions elsewhere in this chapter.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Amphitrichous describes a single flagellum at each of the cell's two poles (two flagella total), not one flagellum at only one pole.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lophotrichous describes a tuft of several flagella at one pole, not a single flagellum.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peritrichous describes flagella distributed all around the cell, not confined to a single pole.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Vibrio cholerae as a classic monotrichous organism (single flagellum, one pole), and distinguish this from amphitrichous, lophotrichous and peritrichous arrangements.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Membrane-active antimicrobials alter selective permeability
questions.question: Antimicrobials that affect bacterial cytoplasmic membrane are going to alter?

explanations.A: Correct. The cytoplasmic membrane's defining function is to act as a selectively permeable barrier, controlling what enters and leaves the cell -- so an antimicrobial that disrupts this membrane directly alters that selective-permeability function, typically by disrupting the lipid bilayer and letting essential ions and metabolites leak out uncontrollably. This is the mechanism of action for membrane-active agents such as polymyxins, distinct from cell-wall-active agents (like beta-lactams, which alter rigidity/shape instead) or ribosome-active agents (which alter protein synthesis, not permeability).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rigidity is provided by the peptidoglycan cell wall, not the cytoplasmic membrane; an agent targeting the membrane does not primarily alter rigidity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Staining affinity depends on the cell wall's peptidoglycan content, not the cytoplasmic membrane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Shape is maintained by the rigid peptidoglycan wall, not the fluid cytoplasmic membrane; membrane-active agents do not primarily alter cell shape.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Antigenicity is largely determined by surface molecules such as LPS, flagella (H antigen) and capsule, not by the cytoplasmic membrane's permeability function.

questions.learning_objective: State that antimicrobials acting on the cytoplasmic membrane alter its selective-permeability function, distinct from wall-active agents (rigidity/shape) or other targets (staining, antigenicity).

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Taxonomy is the science of naming and classifying organisms
questions.question: Nomenclature of living organisms is a science called?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bioinformatics is the computational analysis of biological data (e.g. sequence data); it is a tool sometimes used within modern taxonomy, but it is not itself the science of naming and classifying organisms.
explanations.B: Correct. Taxonomy is specifically the scientific discipline of naming, describing and classifying organisms into a hierarchical, ordered system (e.g. genus and species) -- this naming/classification focus is what distinguishes it from the broader or unrelated fields listed as distractors.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Molecular biology studies biological molecules (DNA, RNA, proteins) and their interactions; it is a distinct discipline from the naming and classification of whole organisms, even though molecular data can inform modern taxonomy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Biology" is the broad overarching science of living organisms in general -- too broad to be the specific answer to "the science of nomenclature," which names a narrower discipline (taxonomy) within biology.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cosmology is the study of the universe's origin and large-scale structure; it has no connection to naming or classifying living organisms.

questions.learning_objective: Identify taxonomy as the science of naming, describing and classifying organisms, distinct from bioinformatics, molecular biology, general biology and cosmology.

questions.title: Bacterial spores are resistant to boiling, not sensitive to it
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a character of bacterial spores?

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement). Spores are indeed markedly dehydrated internally compared with the vegetative cell, which contributes to their heat and desiccation resistance.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). The dense, resistant spore coat does not take up the Gram stain in the usual way, appearing as an unstained, refractile area.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the one that is NOT a character of bacterial spores. Spores are, in fact, highly RESISTANT to boiling, not sensitive to it -- their heat resistance is exactly what makes simple boiling an unreliable sterilisation method against them, requiring autoclaving (pressurised steam above 100C) for reliable destruction.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement). Sporulation typically occurs in the external environment (e.g. soil), outside a host, when nutrients become limited.
explanations.E: Incorrect (true statement). Sporulation is triggered by unfavourable environmental conditions, most classically nutrient limitation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that bacterial spores are resistant (not sensitive) to boiling, while correctly recognising dehydration, Gram-stain negativity, extra-host formation and unfavourable-condition triggers as genuine spore characters.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Gram-negative bacteria + lysozyme yields a spheroplast
questions.question: They are formed from gram negative bacteria if they are treated with lysozyme?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Protoplast is specifically the Gram-positive result of lysozyme treatment (complete wall loss); a Gram-negative cell's outer membrane survives, so it does not become a fully wall-less protoplast.
explanations.B: Correct. Treating a Gram-negative bacterium with lysozyme digests its thin peptidoglycan layer, but the outer membrane survives the treatment, leaving behind a spheroplast -- a cell that has lost its peptidoglycan but retains a residual outer-membrane layer. This is the direct counterpart to the protoplast that results from the same lysozyme treatment applied to a Gram-positive cell, which has no outer membrane to begin with.
explanations.C: Incorrect. L-forms are a broader category of cell-wall-deficient bacteria that can arise from various wall-damaging agents (including antibiotics such as beta-lactams), not the specific name for the lysozyme-on-Gram-negative-cells result.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mycoplasma is a distinct genus that is permanently, genetically wall-less -- it is not a transient state induced by treating a Gram-negative bacterium with lysozyme.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Mycobacteria have an unusual, lipid-rich (mycolic acid) cell wall; lysozyme treatment of a Gram-negative organism does not produce a mycobacterium.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that lysozyme treatment of a Gram-negative bacterium yields a spheroplast (retaining the outer membrane), distinct from a protoplast, L-form, Mycoplasma or Mycobacteria.

questions.title: The bacterial chromosome is circular, not linear
questions.question: What is INCORRECT regarding prokaryotes?

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement). Prokaryotes genuinely lack a nuclear membrane.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). Prokaryotes lack a nucleolus, a eukaryotic nuclear substructure.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the incorrect statement, so it is the INCORRECT answer being asked for. The bacterial chromosome is CIRCULAR, not linear -- describing it as linear reverses the actual, standard feature of bacterial genome organisation.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement). Prokaryotes reproduce by binary fission, a simple splitting into two daughter cells.
explanations.E: Incorrect (true statement). Prokaryotes genuinely lack mitochondria.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that the bacterial chromosome is circular (not linear) among otherwise correct prokaryotic features (no nuclear membrane, no nucleolus, binary fission, no mitochondria).

questions.title: Bacterial spores can be destroyed by autoclaving (121C, ~20 min)
questions.question: The following statement is CORRECT regarding bacterial spores?

options.A: Can be destroyed at 121° C for 20 min

explanations.A: Correct. Bacterial endospores, despite their extraordinary resistance, can be reliably destroyed by autoclaving -- moist heat at around 121C held for roughly 15-20 minutes. This pressurised, sustained heat exposure is what overcomes the spore's dehydrated, chemically resistant coat, unlike simple boiling at 100C, which spores can survive for hours. It is why autoclaving, not simple boiling, is the standard sterilisation method relied on when spores must be eliminated.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sporulation is a survival mechanism in response to adverse conditions, not a method of reproduction -- one cell forms one spore, and spore numbers do not increase relative to the parent population.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The dense, resistant spore coat does not take up the Gram stain in the ordinary way.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sporulation is limited to certain Gram-positive genera (classically Bacillus and Clostridium), not all bacteria.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A spore is not a metabolic dead end -- given favourable conditions, it can germinate (vegetate) back into an active, dividing vegetative cell.

questions.learning_objective: State that autoclaving (about 121C for 15-20 minutes) reliably destroys bacterial spores, rejecting false claims about reproduction, Gram-stain uptake, universality across bacteria, and the inability to germinate.

questions.title: Bacterial endospores form outside the host, inside the bacterium
questions.question: Bacterial endospores are formed?

options.A: Outside the host and outside the bacteria
options.B: Inside the host and inside the bacteria
options.C: Outside the host and inside the bacteria
options.D: Inside the host and outside the bacteria

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Endospore" means the spore forms INSIDE the parent bacterial cell, not outside it -- "outside the bacteria" is wrong regardless of host location.
explanations.B: Incorrect. While sporulation can in principle occur regardless of host presence, classic teaching emphasises environmental (extra-host), nutrient-limited conditions as the typical trigger, not specifically inside a host.
explanations.C: Correct. As the name "endospore" (endo- = within) indicates, the spore forms inside the parent bacterial cell; and classically, sporulation is triggered by nutrient-limited conditions in the external environment -- outside a host -- rather than requiring the presence of a host at all. This combination (outside the host, inside the bacterium) is the standard teaching point about where and how endospores arise.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Endospores form inside, not outside, the bacterial cell -- "outside the bacteria" is wrong regardless of host location.

questions.learning_objective: State that bacterial endospores form inside the parent bacterial cell, typically outside a host, in response to environmental nutrient limitation.

questions.title: Viruses are not true cells
questions.question: True cells include the following EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a genuine true cell, so not the EXCEPT answer). Fungi are eukaryotic organisms made of true cells, with a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the one entry that is NOT a true cell, so it is the EXCEPT answer. A virus is acellular -- an obligate intracellular particle with no independent metabolism, no ribosomes of its own, and no capacity to reproduce outside a host cell's machinery, unlike fungi, bacteria and human cells, which are all independently living, true cellular organisms (eukaryotic or prokaryotic).
explanations.C: Incorrect (genuine true cell). Bacteria are prokaryotic true cells -- they lack a membrane-bound nucleus, but they are independently living cells with their own metabolism and ribosomes.
explanations.D: Incorrect (genuine true cell). Human cells are eukaryotic true cells, with a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles.

questions.learning_objective: Identify viruses as acellular (not true cells), distinguishing them from the true cellular organisms fungi, bacteria and human cells.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Fungi and human cells are eukaryotes
questions.question: Eukaryotes include?

explanations.A: Incorrect alone (and wrong on its own terms). A virus is acellular, not a eukaryote (or any kind of cell) at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bacteria are prokaryotes, not eukaryotes -- they lack a membrane-bound nucleus.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone (true but partial). Fungi are genuinely eukaryotic, but this alone omits the other correct eukaryote in the list (human cells), so it is not the complete answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect alone (true but partial). Human cells are genuinely eukaryotic, but this alone omits fungi, the other correct eukaryote in the list.
explanations.E: Correct. Both fungi and human cells are eukaryotic: each has a true, membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. So "both C, D" is the complete answer, since neither one alone captures every eukaryote in the list. This is unlike bacteria (prokaryotic, no true nucleus) or a virus (not a cell at all, so not a eukaryote either).

questions.learning_objective: Identify fungi and human cells (not bacteria or viruses) as the eukaryotes among the listed options.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: The bacterial cell has one circular chromosome, and no histones
questions.question: Bacterial cell?

options.A: Contain only one type of nucleic acid

explanations.A: Incorrect. A bacterial cell contains both DNA (its genome) and RNA (messenger, ribosomal and transfer RNA for gene expression) -- not only one type of nucleic acid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bacterial cells have no mitochondria at all; respiratory enzymes instead sit in the cytoplasmic membrane.
explanations.C: Correct. The defining feature of a bacterial genome is a single, circular DNA chromosome. It is typically held free in the cytoplasm's nucleoid region rather than enclosed by a nuclear membrane. This single-circular-chromosome pattern is unlike the multiple linear chromosomes packaged inside a eukaryotic nucleus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Most bacteria (the exception being Mycoplasma) do have a cell wall.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Bacterial DNA is not packaged around histone proteins the way eukaryotic chromatin is -- bacteria instead use different DNA-binding proteins (e.g. HU protein) for compaction, and lack true histones.

questions.learning_objective: State that a bacterial cell has a single circular chromosome, and reject false claims about single nucleic-acid type, mitochondria, absent cell wall and histone-associated DNA.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Prokaryotic cells have no true nucleus
questions.question: Prokaryotic cells has no?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Prokaryotic cells do have ribosomes (70S) -- the site of protein synthesis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Most prokaryotic cells do have a cell wall (Mycoplasma being the well-known exception).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Prokaryotic cells do have mesosomes, the classically described cytoplasmic-membrane invaginations housing respiratory enzymes.
explanations.D: Correct. A prokaryotic cell lacks a true, membrane-bound nucleus -- its DNA instead sits free in the cytoplasm's unbound nucleoid region. This is one of the single most defining features that separates a prokaryotic cell from a eukaryotic one, which does enclose its DNA within a true nucleus.

questions.learning_objective: State that a prokaryotic cell lacks a true, membrane-bound nucleus, while possessing ribosomes, (usually) a cell wall, and mesosomes.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Bacteria are prokaryotes
questions.question: Prokaryotes Includes?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fungi are eukaryotic organisms, not prokaryotes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Human cells are eukaryotic, not prokaryotes.
explanations.C: Correct. Bacteria are the classic prokaryotic organisms -- cells with no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles, a single circular chromosome held in the nucleoid, and 70S ribosomes. Among the options given, only bacteria fit the prokaryote category; fungi and human cells are eukaryotic, and a virus is not a cell (prokaryotic or otherwise) at all.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A virus is acellular -- not a prokaryote, not a eukaryote, not any kind of true cell.

questions.learning_objective: State that bacteria are the prokaryotic organisms among fungi, human cells and viruses (eukaryotic and acellular respectively).

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26
